lesson.title: Place Value: Hundreds, Tens, and Ones
lesson.subject: math

contentBlocks.text: Last year you worked with numbers up to 20. This year we're going much bigger — all the way to 1,000! To work with big numbers, you need a powerful tool: place value.

Every digit in a number has a place, and that place tells you its value. In the number 342, the 3 is in the hundreds place (worth 300), the 4 is in the tens place (worth 40), and the 2 is in the ones place (worth 2). Add those together: 300 + 40 + 2 = 342. Try breaking apart 256 the same way: 2 hundreds, 5 tens, 6 ones.
Understanding place value is the key to everything we'll do with bigger numbers this year. Tomorrow we'll use it to add two-digit numbers.

objectives: Identify the value of each digit in a three-digit number (hundreds, tens, ones place)
Decompose a three-digit number into hundreds + tens + ones
materialsNeeded: Printed 'Place Value: Hundreds, Tens, and Ones' worksheet
Optional: base-ten blocks or grouped objects (10 groups of 10) for a hands-on model
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Write 342 and ask the child what each digit might mean.
2. Introduce the three places: hundreds, tens, ones, and their values.
3. Model breaking apart 342 into 300+40+2 together.
4. Practice with 256 and one more number together.
5. Move to the worksheet: break apart each number into hundreds, tens, and ones.
6. Close by asking the child to build a number of their own choosing and explain its place values.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use physical base-ten blocks or bundled objects (10 sticks bundled as a ten, 10 bundles as a hundred) to make place value concrete
Ready for more: ask what happens to a number's value if you swap two digits (e.g. 342 vs 432) — why does order matter so much?
For a visual learner, draw each number as hundreds/tens/ones blocks before writing the breakdown
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. 342 = 3 hundreds, 4 tens, 2 ones. 2. 256 = 2 hundreds, 5 tens, 6 ones. 3. 189 = 1 hundred, 8 tens, 9 ones. 4. 705 = 7 hundreds, 0 tens, 5 ones.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Place value understanding for three-digit numbers is the core Grade 2 foundation (matching Common Core 2.NBT.1) that all of this week's addition and subtraction strategies build directly on.
